stops.name: Berlin, a dancer is born
stops.campa: Elsa Lindenberg is born in Berlin in 1906, a daughter of the working city: the Berlin of tenement courtyards, factory whistles and Sunday allotments. The capital she enters is about to become the capital of the dancing body: within her childhood Berlin will fill with movement choirs, gymnastic reformers and barefoot prophets, and the canon of German dance will count her among its emigrant daughters. From the beginning the family has little money, and the child has one estate only: a body that listens.

stops.name: Berlin, the Helene Lange school, the scholarship child
stops.campa: Thirteen years old, Elsa enters the Helene Lange school in Berlin as a scholarship pupil, and her dance training begins. It is 1919: the Kaiser is gone, the Republic is hungry, and the city's answer to hunger is movement: Ausdruckstanz, the expression-dance, is being invented street by street. A scholarship child among the daughters of the Bürgertum, she earns her place with her body. The training is disciplined and free of charge, and she will never afterwards dance for anyone who has not earned her yes.

stops.name: Halensee, the villa of Hertha Feist, the Laban school
stops.campa: In a villa in Halensee, Elsa enrolls in the school of Hertha Feist, Laban's apostle in Berlin: the school for body-culture and dance where movement choirs, gymnastics, sunlight and the master's swings and scales make a single doctrine of the body. Here she takes the Laban training entire: space-harmony, effort, the body as a crystal of directions. She completes her diploma in 1927. The lineage is exact: Laban to Feist to Elsa, the mountain of Monte Verità come down to a Berlin garden.

stops.name: Charlottenburg, the Städtische Oper, the corps de ballet
stops.campa: Diploma in hand, she is engaged as a group dancer in the ballet of the Städtische Oper on the Bismarckstraße, and for six seasons the scholarship girl dances in the great house of Charlottenburg. The corps is discipline made nightly flesh: swan maidens, temple dancers, the operatic underworld. In these same years Laban himself ascends to the Prussian State Theatres across town; the new dance and the old house negotiate nightly in her joints. By day she goes looking for other rooms and other teachers.

stops.name: Berlin, the quiet room of Elsa Gindler
stops.campa: In a quiet Berlin studio Elsa finds the other pole of her art: Elsa Gindler, who teaches almost nothing and changes everything: sitting, standing, breathing attended to until the body reorganizes itself from within. Gindler writes nothing down; the work passes hand to hand like a rite. Lindenberg becomes her student and remains one across the ruin of the century, before the war and after it. Between Laban's great spatial crystals and Gindler's microscopic attention, the dancer now holds both ends of the body's knowledge.

stops.name: Wilmersdorf, the Künstlerkolonie, the Red Block
stops.campa: She lives among the writers and artists of the Künstlerkolonie at the Laubenheimer Platz in Wilmersdorf, and she is a Communist: a member of the Red Block cell of the colony, the red island Arthur Koestler will remember in The God That Failed. The dancers' Berlin and the workers' Berlin are one city in her. Nights of meetings, leaflets, watchfulness against the SA squads that raid the colony; days in the opera's rehearsal rooms. The Party knows her as dedicated and courageous; the police begin to know her too.

stops.name: Berlin by night, the glue-pot and the posters
stops.campa: By night the dancer of the Städtische Oper walks the dark streets with a pot of glue and a roll of posters against Hitler, pasting the walls of Berlin with warnings. It is dangerous work, the SA also walks at night, and it is in this underground weather that the name of Wilhelm Reich first reaches her: the Party doctor who preaches that fascism is made in the body, in the strangled life of the masses. She has heard of him before she ever sees him.
stops.quote: I got to know Willie Reich when I used to walk around Berlin at night with a pot of glue and anti-Hitler posters.
stops.quote_source: Elsa Lindenberg, filmed recollection, quoted at Spartacus Educational, 'Elsa Lindenberg'

stops.name: Berlin, the May march, the meeting with Reich
stops.campa: On a Communist march in May, Elsa and Dr. Wilhelm Reich walk in the same column, and the attraction between them is immediate and admitted. He is the founder of Sex-Pol, analyst of the Berlin clinics, author of banned enlightenments; he is also married. They begin seeing each other regularly, and the affair is no secret. She is troubled by the falseness of the position and says so, for clarity is her nature. The canon marks this column of marchers as the meeting place of psychoanalysis and the dance.

stops.name: Berlin, the meeting with Annie Reich
stops.campa: Elsa will not live in a lie: she asks for and gets a face-to-face meeting with Annie Reich, wife of the man she loves. The two women sit opposite one another in the failing marriage's parlor and speak plainly. Annie, who has known other affairs and knows this one is different, essentially surrenders her hold, and afterwards writes to Elsa a single sentence: that Elsa's happiness will be built upon her tears. The sentence is kept, and the marriage dies through the winter.

stops.name: Berlin, the night of the burning Reichstag
stops.campa: On the night of the twenty-seventh of February the Reichstag burns, and the Republic's ashes are used to bury the Republic. Reich, just returned from Denmark, sees the fire and understands; within days he is over the border. Elsa remains in the trap of Berlin: she has a contract, a family, a cell, a life. Between them now travel letters: he bombards her with pleas to come to Vienna, where his wife and children are; she refuses the triangle flatly. She will come to him free or not at all.

stops.name: Charlottenburg, cast out of the Opera
stops.campa: The new Reich reaches into the opera house: on the twenty-first of April Elsa Lindenberg is formally expelled from the ballet of the Städtische Oper under the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service, charged with conduct damaging to the state. The state is correct: she has damaged it with glue and posters and will damage it more. With Ruth Abramowitsch and Ilse Larede she has stood against the brownshirts; now come the search of her apartment, the warrant, and the end of the Berlin stage.

stops.name: Stettiner Bahnhof, the road north
stops.campa: In late May she chooses: not Vienna and the ménage, but Copenhagen and the man alone. From the Stettiner Bahnhof the trains run north to the ferries. She leaves the city of her whole life: school, villa, opera, colony, the walls she postered, carrying the two Berlins in her body, Laban's and Gindler's, the stage and the street. The Gestapo keeps her file open. Elsa Lindenberg goes into an exile that will last, with a few burning returns, the rest of her life.
